entry.title: Agentic AI Needs an Environment: Lessons from PaPM and ERP Controlling
entry.content:
For an AI to be truly agentic, it needs an environment to work in. To me, this is almost self-evident.

Connecting an LLM to data is not enough. The environment needs state, business logic, functions the agent can call, and a way to receive feedback from a human. Only then can the AI do more than answer a question. It can move toward a goal: look at what is happening, decide what to do next, run the right function, inspect the result, spot a problem, form a hypothesis, and test it.

By this definition, both a calculation model in SAP Profitability and Performance Management (PaPM) and the Controlling module in ERP can serve as environments for agentic AI.

1. The PaPM calculation model as an environment

In PaPM, the calculation is stored in a narrative form. Functions embed the methodology, and the methodology consists of a preparation phase and the factor analysis calculation itself.

So where does the agentic part come in? I don’t see our agent as a chat that looks at a final table and writes a nicely worded report. Imagine it receives a task: run the calculation and analyze the significant variances for a specific production order. The agent then works out the steps on its own. It prepares the required data, runs the right functions, executes the calculation, looks at the result, and only then starts analyzing. Along the way it can:

  • determine which preparation functions need to run,
  • execute the right sequence of functions,
  • retrieve the result,
  • walk through the final table and find significant variances,
  • identify which factor drove each variance,
  • trace back through the model and methodology to understand how the number was produced,
  • prepare a final report for the user.

Suppose the agent notices that the standard price differs sharply from the actual one. It digs into the drivers and finds that one factor is the number of hours: 170 working hours were expected, but only 10 hours were allocated to this production order.

Context matters here. We are looking at a single production order, but cost allocation happens during period-end closing. If more production orders had been closed in the period, the costs (specifically labor costs) would have been spread across them, and the result for this order would look different.

So the agent doesn’t just say, “You have 170 planned hours against 10 actual.” It explains why this affected the result and how the figure connects to the calculation methodology: the gap between expected and allocated hours changed the cost distribution and, in turn, the outcome of the factor analysis.

When the model isn’t enough

Sometimes the information inside the PaPM model is not sufficient to find the real cause. This is where I also see agentic behavior. The agent must not invent a cause and present it as fact. It should say something like:

“A possible reason is how the actual production time was recorded in ERP.” (a hypothesis)

Then it needs to figure out how to verify that hypothesis, and tell the human where to look:

“Check production order X in ERP. Review the confirmed production time and the source it came from in the calculation.”

The agent is no longer just answering a question. It is directing a person to what needs to be checked. The person goes to ERP, confirms or rejects the hypothesis, and the loop continues.

This points to an important architectural principle. ERP is our source of truth, so the LLM must never decide on its own that a hypothesis is a fact. Once a human confirms the cause, we can use that information going forward. And we don’t necessarily need to copy ERP data into PaPM or replicate anything. We can create a new view on the PaPM side that gives the agent access to the relevant ERP information. Next time, the agent can consult that source and include it in its analysis.

The full cycle looks like this:

calculation result → model analysis → missing information → hypothesis → next step → verification in ERP → human confirmation → new access to the needed information → next analysis with that context

That, for me, is where agentic AI appears. Not in the LLM’s ability to write fluent text, but in the agent’s ability to understand what to do next, what information it lacks, where to go, what to check, and how to continue once it has an answer. The agent can also do more than analyze a finished result. It can run the calculation itself by executing the sequence of methodology functions in PaPM.

2. The Controlling module in ERP

In ERP this is, in my view, even more obvious. The agent operates inside the system that is the source of truth. It knows which controlling tables exist, what they mean, how they relate, which processes exist, and which functions it can call. So it can perform concrete tasks, not just analyze:

  • create a cost center,
  • check an existing cost center,
  • validate an allocation function,
  • verify that data is configured correctly,
  • execute period-end closing steps,
  • work with reporting and the Review Booklet,
  • search for root causes of variances.

Period-end closing shows this best. The goal is simple to state: close the period. But that is not a single function call. It is a sequence of actions: check that all prerequisites are met, including settlement, then check the data, find errors or blockers, run the necessary functions, verify again, and move on.

When something goes wrong, the agent must decide what to do next. For example:

closing → error in allocation → analyze the allocation function → find a missing cost center → depending on what is being allocated, determine which master data is missing → fix it → rerun allocation → check the result → continue closing

This shows what agentic means: goal → planning → action → observe the outcome → decide what’s next → revise the plan if needed.

Our PaPM agent does exactly the same thing. The difference is only in which functions it runs. In ERP, they belong to a business process such as period closing. In PaPM, they belong to the calculation model, accessed through Joule for PaPM and then through Joule Work, a kind of universal workstation connected to the different systems in the landscape.

3. So what is the difference between PaPM and ERP?

For me, the difference is not that one scenario is agentic and the other isn’t. Both can be. The environments are simply different.

In ERP, the agent sits where the business state and the source of truth live, so it doesn’t need extra views to reach the root cause. In PaPM, the agent has the calculation model, methodology, functions, and results, but part of the information needed to explain a root cause lives in ERP. At some point the agent may conclude: “I understand the calculation, but I lack the information to explain the cause.” Then it has to go further.

Put simply:

  • ERP tells us what is happening in the business.
  • PaPM shows how the calculated result was produced.
  • The agent works out why the result looks the way it does, what is missing, and what to do next.

Why this is more than an “analytical assistant”

I wouldn’t call this agent merely an analytical assistant. Yes, it helps users with analytics, but the core idea is different.

Today, a person walks through multiple transactions, exports several Excel files, compares tables, calculates things, finds a variance, goes to another system to verify the cause, and finally assembles a report. The point of an agent is to take the human out of that routine sequence of actions.

The same goal applies to an agent handling period closing. Today a person runs the functions, checks the results, hunts for errors, and decides what to do next. The agent should do that work instead.

That is why I see no fundamental difference between these two flows:

closing → run allocation → check → run settlement → check → finish closing

run PaPM preparation phase → run calculation → review result → find variance → understand cause → request additional information → verify it → continue analysis

Behaviorally, it is the same logic: there is a goal, there is a set of available actions, and the agent chooses what to do next, observes the result, and continues.

This is also why I believe that preparing an important prerequisite for the calculation with a colleague was a real step forward. Yes, a person can walk through transactions and export a number of Excel files to build a report. But then the question is: why do we need an agent at all? The answer is that a person should no longer have to do this. The agent should own the whole process.

The idea may not have been fully understood at first, because it is somewhat indirect. I am not trying to build yet another chat that tells users a nice story about what happened. I want an assistant that performs the sequence of actions a human performs today.

The LLM is there to understand context, interpret information, form hypotheses, decide on next steps, and connect different sources. ERP and PaPM remain the systems that hold the business itself and the calculation logic.

That is why I see agentic AI as an intelligent layer on top of existing systems, not a replacement for them. That, in the end, is the whole point.

entry.title: Teched2026-XP266 -- Ship your own sandboxed AI operations agent to Kyma in two hours
entry.content:
Bring your own agent to a contained SAP Kyma sandbox with OpenRouter

Plug OpenRouter - a public LLM aggregator - into a contained sandbox with three off-the-shelf coding agents powered by free NVIDIA Nemotron models

This is a follow-up to Teched2026-XP266 | Giving an AI agent a shell — without giving away the keys to your cluster.
That post built the contained sandbox on SAP Kyma: the box is the boundary, three trust tiers, and an agent that reasons through a frontier model it never holds the key to.
Here we add a fourth tier — an external provider — and run somebody else's coding agents on a free public model, without loosening a single guarantee.

TL;DR

  • The sandbox model generalizes. "The in-cluster LLM proxy" was never special — it was just one provider. Swap in OpenRouter (a public aggregator) and the box behaves identically: one allow-listed host, nothing else.
  • Bring the model, not the key. The real OpenRouter key lives only in the gateway. Inside the box the agent carries a sentinel; the supervisor swaps it for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary → a listed host.
  • Three off-the-shelf agents, one image, a free model. opencode, Pi, and Qwen Code — all pointed at free NVIDIA Nemotron models on OpenRouter.
  • Containment holds with a public host in the mix. The box reaches openrouter.ai and nothing else — not the internet at large, not the API server. We prove it with three curls.
  • "External" isn't "less contained." Opening one host for named binaries, with the key injected at the wire, is a different tier — not a looser one.
  • The abstraction was the product. The sandbox never cared whether the model was in-cluster or across the planet; "provider" is the seam, and it holds.
  • A free model is a confident junior. Great for a first draft, wrong about anything niche — so make the cluster the reviewer, not the reader.

Contents

  • ⚖️ The itch
  • 🧭 The fourth tier
  • 👀 See it first
  • 🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox
  • 🔍 The deep dive
    • 3a. The profile is the policy
    • 3b. The provider holds the key
    • 3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel
    • 3d. Picking a free model
  • ️🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix
  • 🎯 Why it's worth it
  • 🧰 Reusable patterns
  • 📎 Appendix
  • 📚 References & BOM
  • 📖 Lexicon
  • 🎓 See it live — SAP TechEd 2026 (XP266)

⚖️ The itch — one more model, one more key

👉The first post left the agent talking to SAP AI Core, in-cluster, through an in-cluster LLM proxy — no key in the box, no route to the internet.

👉However, sooner or later someone will need a feature the in-cluster proxy doesn't bridge yet, for instance:

  • a public aggregator,
  • a shiny free model to prototype with,
  • an off-the-shelf coding agent that only knows how to talk to OpenRouter.

👉So the question remains:

How do you let an agent use an external model — reached over the public internet — without putting the key in the box or opening a route it can abuse?

👉The answer turns out to be not a new mechanism at all.

🧭 The fourth tier — an external provider

The first post had three tiers — the same sandbox image, with each tier granting a bit more access - the more you trust the workload. 

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
1. Containedthe in-cluster LLM onlynonenone (sentinel)
2. Scoped-ops+ API server (read-only)read-only kubectlnone (sentinel)
3. Web terminalfull pod networkRBAC-scoped kubectlnone (sentinel)

This external provider adds a fourth tier — same pattern adding one more row:

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
4. External agentone public host (openrouter.ai)nonenone (sentinel)

👉And it is not a weaker tier — it's a different one.

  • The box still can't reach the API server or the rest of the internet. 
  • And the only thing that changed is which single endpoint the supervisor opens, and that the credential behind it is a real OpenRouter key — held, as always, by the gateway and never by the box.

👀 See it first — from the web terminal

  • Kyma web terminal embeds the openshell CLI
  • the terminal runs inside the cluster, thus, you reach the gateway's Service directly (no HTTPS host, no port-forward).
  • The openshell gateway is OIDC-gated; it validates your Keycloak token itself.
  • The terminal has no browser, so you log in with the device-code flow:

 

export XP266_CLUSTER=xp266-NNN          # your runtime number
export XP266_DOMAIN=<workshop-domain>   # handed out at the session

OPENSHELL_NO_BROWSER=1 openshell gateway add http://openshell.openshell.svc.cluster.local:8080 \
  --oidc-issuer https://keycloak.$XP266_CLUSTER.$XP266_DOMAIN/realms/ateam-isveng \
  --oidc-client-id openshell-oidc
#   To authenticate, visit:
#     https://keycloak.<cluster>.<domain>/realms/ateam-isveng/device?user_code=XXXX-XXXX
#   ✓ Authenticated via device code      ← approve on your laptop, you need the `openshell-admin` role

👉pick a current free model and create the sandbox:

 

export FREE_MODEL=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free   # a current :free NVIDIA model

openshell sandbox create --name agents \
  --from localhost:32137/openrouter-agents:latest \
  --provider openrouter \
  --env OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 \
  --env OPENAI_MODEL=$FREE_MODEL \
  --detach -- sleep infinity &
openshell sandbox list        # wait for PHASE=Ready
👉--provider openrouter is the whole trick: it opens egress to openrouter.ai (+ models.dev) for the agent binaries only, and injects the key sentinel.

👉Run any of the three agents — same box, same model:

# opencode (open-source Bun agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- opencode run -m openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "Reply with one word: PONG"
#   PONG

# Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- pi -p --model openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "List 3 facts about Kyma."

# Qwen Code (OpenAI-compatible — takes no -m; reads $OPENAI_MODEL):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- qwen -p "List 3 facts about Kyma."
 

👉An off-the-shelf coding agent just reasoned through a frontier-grade free model.

Now the punchline: try to break out

openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- sh -c '
  curl -sS -m8 -o /dev/null -w "openrouter.ai: %{http_code}\n" https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models
  curl -sS -m8 https://example.com            >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "example.com: REACHED" || echo "example.com: blocked"
  curl -sS -m8 https://kubernetes.default.svc >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "apiserver: REACHED"   || echo "apiserver: blocked"
  echo "key in box: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
 
openrouter.ai: 200
example.com: blocked                     ← the rest of the internet: no route
apiserver: blocked                       ← the cluster API: no route
key in box: openshell:resolve:env:…      ← a sentinel, NOT the real key

👉One host reachable.

  • ✅Everything else refused.
  • ✅The key never in the box.
  • ✅That's the fourth tier in three curl lines.

🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox

Three concepts, one key that never leaves the gateway:

  • Profile — a reusable spec, no secret in it: which credential env var, which auth style, which endpoints egress may reach, and which binaries are allowed to use the credential.
  • Provider — a profile bound to a real key. The key (sk-or-…) is stored only in the gateway.
  • Sandbox — --provider openrouter attaches it: the box receives a sentinel (not the key) + scoped egress; the supervisor swaps the sentinel for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary reaching a listed endpoint.
 

 

Same picture, in ASCII, for renderers that don't do Mermaid:

   ┌───────────────── OpenShell gateway (holds the real key) ───────────────── ┐
   │ profile "openrouter"   credential: OPENROUTER_API_KEY (bearer)            │
   │                        endpoints : openrouter.ai, models.dev  ← only hosts│
   │                        binaries  : node, opencode, qwen, pi   ← only these│
   │ provider "openrouter" = profile + REAL KEY           ← key lives ONLY here│
   └───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                 sandbox create --provider openrouter
                                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────── your sandbox (the box) ────────────────────┐
   │ OPENROUTER_API_KEY = openshell:resolve:…   ← a SENTINEL        │
   │ agent  ──▶  Authorization: Bearer <sentinel>                   │
   └───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                        ▼ (allowed binary + allowed host)
            supervisor swaps  <sentinel> → sk-or-…  AT THE WIRE
                                        ▼
                                  openrouter.ai   (sees the real key; the box never did)
 
In a nutshell:
  • 👉The gateway is the keeper of secrets
  • 👉the profile is the policy
  • 👉the sentinel is what the agent gets instead of a key.

🔍 The deep dive

3a. The profile is the policy (endpoints × binaries)

  • A profile answers two questions and nothing else: which hosts may this credential reach, and which binaries may send that traffic.
  • For OpenRouter that's openrouter.ai (the inference API) plus models.dev (opencode's model-registry metadata, dialed on startup), and the agent binaries (node, opencode, qwen, pi).
  • Everything outside that cross product is denied by default — a block-list would be a guessing game; an allow-list is a decision you can read.

3b. The provider holds the key — once, in one place

  • The provider is the profile plus a real key.
  • On OpenShell 0.1.1 the key is injected into the box as a resolve-sentinel (openshell:resolve:env:…); the supervisor resolves it to the real sk-or-… only at egress, and only for an allowed binary → an allowed host.
  • The two env vars the agents read — OPENROUTER_API_KEY (Pi, opencode) and OPENAI_API_KEY (the OpenAI-compatible Qwen Code) — both carry the sentinel.
  • Compromise the agent and all you've got is the string openshell:resolve:env:….

3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel, never the secret

  • This is the same credential-injection trick from the first post, now across a public hop instead of an in-cluster one.
  • The box's view of the world: an env var that looks like a key but isn't, and exactly one host it's allowed to send it to.
  • The agent can't tell the difference — it sets Authorization: Bearer <sentinel> and the reply comes back — but an attacker who owns the agent gets a placeholder and a single, logged, allow-listed destination.

3d. Picking a free model

OpenRouter's :free tier includes NVIDIA's Nemotron family — frontier-grade, no quota spent.

  • The agents call tools, so the model must be a chat/completion model with tool-calling. Embedding/rerank models (ids with -embed- / -rerank-) are RAG parts, not chat — the agent will error.
  • Two known-good picks: nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free (large, higher quality) and nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free (smaller, faster).

🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix

  • 👉 The instinct is that "the box can now reach the internet" must mean "the box is less safe."
  • 👉 It doesn't — because the internet was never opened.

Here's what each familiar threat runs into:

ThreatWhat usually enables itWhat this tier does instead
Data exfiltrationthe agent has the internetone host resolves (openrouter.ai); example.com and everything else → no route
Reaching the clusterpod → API server pathno route to kubernetes.default.svc — this tier grants no cluster access at all
Credential theftthe agent holds the keythe key is never in the box — a sentinel in, the real sk-or-… injected at the last hop
A rogue binary phoning homeany process can egressegress is binary-scoped — only node/opencode/qwen/pi may send; anything else is denied
Silent abuseno audit trailevery denied request is logged at the supervisor

 

 

🎯 Why it's worth it

You can say yes to a much wider set of "can the agent use this model?" questions, because "use" now happens somewhere it can't hurt you — even when the model lives on the public internet behind a paid key:

  • ✅ off-the-shelf coding agents (opencode, Pi, Qwen Code) you didn't write and don't fully trust, run safely
  • ✅ free models for prototyping and workshops — no quota, no standing credential in the box
  • ✅ the same contained guarantees as the in-cluster tier: one host, no cluster, key in the gateway
  • ✅ a clean generalization — "provider" means any governed endpoint, in-cluster or external, by the same rules

All on the stock OpenShell chart and agent-sandbox controller, on a normal managed Kyma cluster.

🧰 Reusable patterns

Strip out OpenRouter and several of these stand on their own — a toolkit for governing any external dependency a semi-trusted workload needs.

  • Model the credential as a profile, not an env var. Separate the spec (which hosts, which binaries, which auth) from the secret. The spec is reviewable in Git; the secret lives in exactly one guarded place. ✅ You can audit "what can reach the internet" without ever seeing a key.
  •  Scope egress by binary, not just by host. "node and opencode may reach openrouter.ai" is a far tighter statement than "the pod may reach openrouter.ai." A rogue process in the box still can't send. ✅ Lateral egress inside the box is closed, not just lateral network.
  • Inject credentials at the wire — even across a public hop. The workload carries a sentinel; the proxy swaps in the real value on the last hop out. Works identically whether the destination is in-cluster or on the internet. ✅ Compromise the workload and the attacker gets the word "placeholder".
  • One proxy, two shapes. OpenAI-compatible gateways (SAP AI Core, OpenRouter) look the same to a proxy — so one in-cluster exit can front both, spend-tracked, keys never leaving it. ✅ Add a provider without adding an egress path.
  • Free tiers make experimentation cheap — pin against their churn. A :free model is perfect for a workshop or a spike; its instability is the price. Keep a fallback and list-before-you-run. ✅ Zero-cost iteration, with a documented escape hatch when a model goes paid.
  • Let the platform adjudicate generated code. For anything an LLM writes against a niche API, make the API server the gate: --dry-run=server before trust. The draft→reject→fix loop is the workflow. ✅ The model's confidence stops mattering; the cluster's acceptance is the only verdict.

👉The recipe, in one line:

credential-as-profile → binary-scoped egress → sentinel-at-the-wire → one proxy, two shapes → free tier with a fallback → the cluster adjudicates generated code.

📎 Appendix

 

A. The provider profile (what --provider openrouter binds to)

Wired once per gateway (the real key is handed to the gateway here and never leaves it):

  • The profile lists the endpoints egress may reach (openrouter.ai, models.dev) and the binaries allowed to use the credential; the provider is that profile plus the real sk-or-….
  • Inside the box the agents see only the sentinel in OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY;
  • The supervisor resolves it at egress for an allowed binary → an allowed host.

The profile itself (imported into the gateway) — the whole policy is the endpoint × binary cross-product:

 

id: openrouter
display_name: OpenRouter
inference_capable: true
credentials:
  - name: api_key
    env_vars: [OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY]   # agents read either; injected as a resolve-sentinel, swapped at egress
    auth_style: bearer
    header_name: authorization
endpoints:
  - { host: openrouter.ai, port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-write }   # the inference API (/api/v1/…)
  - { host: models.dev,    port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-only }    # opencode's model registry (dialed on startup)
binaries:
  - /usr/local/bin/node                                        # Pi + Qwen Code — the connecting process is node
  - /usr/local/bin/opencode                                    # opencode launcher symlink
  - /usr/local/lib/node_modules/opencode-ai/bin/opencode.exe   # opencode's RESOLVED Bun ELF (the symlink alone fails)

Why both OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY?

👉 Because the three agents expect the key under different env-var names, and listing both makes the gateway inject the sentinel under each — so whichever name an agent reads, it finds it:

  • OPENROUTER_API_KEY → Pi and opencode (OpenRouter-native).
  • OPENAI_API_KEY → Qwen Code, which is an OpenAI-compatible client and reads the OpenAI name.

Binding the real key turns the profile into a provider: 

The key is read from an in-cluster Secret and handed to the gateway once — it is stored only there, and every sandbox created --provider openrouter receives the sentinel, never the key.

(No tls: on the endpoints — the supervisor terminates TLS transparently and injects a CA bundle: CURL_CA_BUNDLE / NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS.)

 

B. The tools image — built in-cluster by kaniko

openrouter-agents:latest is built inside the cluster by kaniko (no CI, no registry credentials), from a Dockerfile that lives inline in a ConfigMap.

The three agents are the whole payload:

FROM node:24-bookworm-slim
# bash + CA certs for TLS to openrouter.ai; fd + ripgrep pre-installed so the agents' search tools work WITHOUT
# sandbox-blocked downloads; git for repo awareness; curl.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      bash ca-certificates fd-find git ripgrep curl \
 && ln -s /usr/bin/fdfind /usr/local/bin/fd && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# Pi + Qwen Code — pure-JS, installed with --ignore-scripts (supply-chain hygiene, no postinstall):
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@latest"
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@qwen-code/qwen-code@latest"
# opencode — postinstall ALLOWED so it fetches the correct glibc platform binary for this base → /usr/local/bin/opencode:
RUN npm install -g --allow-scripts=opencode-ai "opencode-ai@latest"
# OpenShell 0.1.x runs the sandbox as uid 10001: add a passwd entry so $USER/$HOME resolve + a writable home:
RUN echo 'agent:x:10001:0:agent sandbox:/home/agent:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd \
 && mkdir -p /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent && chmod -R 0777 /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent
WORKDIR /home/agent
ENV PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=/tmp/pi-agent
 

C. OpenRouter vs SAP AI Core — the same shape

Why does an external provider slot in so cleanly?

  • Because OpenRouter and SAP AI Core are the same shape to a proxy: an OpenAI-compatible gateway behind one credential.
  • OpenRouter is a public aggregator (one endpoint, many upstreams — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Qwen, NVIDIA…)
  • SAP AI Core is SAP's managed inference gateway, reached in-cluster through a proxy.

So OpenRouter is just another provider — no new integration, the same sentinel-at-the-wire mechanism.

 SAP AI Core (via in-cluster LLM proxy)OpenRouter (via direct path)
Pathagent → in-cluster proxy → SAP AI Coreagent → OpenRouter (one allow-listed external host)
Key in boxnone — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)none — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)
Internetnoneone host: openrouter.ai

In summary:

  • 👉The key story is identical — in both, the real credential lives only in the gateway and the box carries a sentinel.
  • 👉The only things that differ are the egress path (an in-cluster service vs one public host) and whether any internet is opened at all.
  • ⚠️The one thing that does not work: OpenRouter cannot call SAP AI Core. OpenRouter only routes to its own public upstreams — it can't reach an in-cluster proxy.

📚References & BOM

The exact versions this ran on a managed SAP Kyma TechEd fleet:

📖 Lexicon

TermWhat it means
Provider / profileA profile is a reusable spec — which hosts egress may reach, which binaries may use a credential, which auth style. A provider is a profile bound to a real key. The key lives only in the gateway.
SentinelThe placeholder the box gets instead of the key (openshell:resolve:env:…). The supervisor swaps it for the real key at the last hop out, only for an allowed binary → an allowed host.

entry.title: AI Product Management: Not Every Decision Needs a Language Model
entry.content:
AI Product Management: Not Every Decision Needs a Language Model

I work on SAP Business Data Cloud. The experiment below is a personal project on my own laptop and my own data; the opinions are mine.

Most of the AI features being specified in enterprise software right now share one shape. A row arrives, an invoice, a lead, a purchase order, a service ticket, and the system has to decide something about it: approve or hold, route or escalate, likely late or likely on time. That is classification, the oldest problem in software, and in 2026 the first instinct of almost every team I meet is to hand it to a language model.

I spent the past month testing that instinct on a problem of my own, and I want to share what the numbers said, because they changed how I think about the architecture of an SAP AI feature.

The problem

A family member lost his job this summer, partly to an agent, so I built him one. It reads a few hundred job postings a day, decides which deserve his attention, and matches the survivors against his real history. Triage and matching. He has labeled 2,458 postings as yes or no over six weeks, across 398 employers, which makes it a small, messy, opinionated table of exactly the kind that sits inside every SAP system: a label column that encodes one person's judgment.

The first version used a language model for everything. Within a week I had the failure modes anyone who has shipped an LLM feature will recognize: the same posting judged differently on Tuesday, a confidence score that meant nothing against my labels, a fluent paragraph explaining why a "Production Technician" role was a product role. So I stopped asking how to prompt better and asked the architecture question: should this step be a language model at all.

The landscape experiment

The traditional way to answer that is a diagram. Read the analyst reports, attend two briefings, draw boxes labeled Retrieval, Ranking, Classification, LLM, get approval for a proof of concept that tests one box per sprint and chooses the rest on faith. The diagram is the deliverable because the evidence is unaffordable.

With a coding agent doing the typing and me doing the judging, the evidence became affordable. Over one weekend in September I ran eleven technologies and eight language models on the same labeled postings: dense embeddings with a logistic head, SetFit, XGBoost, a LambdaMART ranker, BM25, a cross-encoder, zero-shot entailment, and language models from a 27B running locally to the most expensive frontier APIs. A logistic regression won, at 0.912 AUC, for a cost of nothing. Zero-shot entailment, the technique that sounds most like what you want, scored a coin flip. Each of those experiments would have taken days the old way; the whole table took less than a weekend.

Then few days ago SAP's CTO posted the NeurIPS list from the tabular AI teams, and I realized I had never tested the one category built for my problem: a tabular foundation model.

The rematch

TabPFN-3.5 is not a language model. It is a transformer trained on millions of synthetic tables and never on internet text. It does not generate anything. Show it labeled rows and it returns a calibrated probability for the unlabeled ones in a single pass, with no training step, no feature engineering, no prompt. I ran the open-weight base model on my laptop, handed it the seven features my hand-built ranker already used plus the raw posting title and description as text columns, and tested it the way I would want to be tested: every posting from a given employer held out together, five folds, five seeds, so the model is never judged on a company it has seen.

It scored first. The logistic regression that had won in September came second, clearly behind. Then I put it against the 46 language-model configurations the pipeline had already stored on the same postings over six weeks, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, each on 958 labeled postings. It was ahead of all of them, clearly, with employers held out.

Method Gap to TabPFN (AUC) Time per 1,000 Cost per 1,000
 

 

Two honest limits. On a time-ordered split, where the model learns only from older postings and is judged on newer ones, the frontier models catch up to a tie; they know things about the world that my labeled history does not. And the open weights are licensed for evaluation, not production; the commercial path is TabPFN-3.5 Plus in SAP AI Core, which I did not use. What held for every model I ran: cost more, took longer, at best matched.

What this means for an SAP AI feature

Three numbers from that table matter more than the AUC to anyone specifying a feature on S/4HANA, SuccessFactors or Ariba.

Twelve seconds per thousand rows means the score fits inside the transaction rather than in a nightly batch. A late-payment probability that takes a quarter of an hour per thousand invoices is a report; one that takes twelve seconds is a column in the work list, refreshed as the data changes.

No training step and no prompt means the person who owns the business decision can run the experiment. A product manager with the labeled rows and a laptop gets the answer before the architecture review is on the calendar.

And a model that reads tables is only as good as the table. TabPFN's input is a governed, entity-grained, point-in-time-correct table with a label column someone owns, which is to say a data product. SAP-RPT-1 goes further and reads the column semantics. That is the strongest argument I have found for the Business Data Cloud approach, and also its sharpest test: the data product that feeds a dashboard can tolerate a stale join or a leaked future column; a tabular model will score beautifully on it and fail in production. Prediction-ready data products need a discipline analytical ones never did.

The architect's new job

The role never was about the diagram. The diagram was a compression artifact, a way of communicating a judgment when the judgment could not be shown. What changed is that the judgment can now be exercised on evidence, by one person, before the steering committee meets. A failed experiment used to be a wasted sprint. Now it is the cheapest line on the invoice, and it is also the deliverable.

So before the next AI feature is specified as "LLM-based," run the table. Rules, then classifiers, then rankers, then tabular models, then generative models, each on the same labeled rows, with accuracy, latency and cost in three columns. It takes a weekend. For the decision that is a row with a label, the right model may be the one that cannot write a sentence.

The full table

Every language model that judged at least 200 of the labeled postings, one row per model at its best configuration, with the number of configurations tried alongside. Each row is scored on exactly the postings that model judged, companies held out, so the TabPFN column moves with the row. Gap is model minus TabPFN; negative means TabPFN was ahead, and the verdict says whether the 95 percent interval excludes zero. Time is wall-clock per 1,000 postings on the hardware the model ran on.

Model Configs AUC model / TabPFN Gap Verdict s per 1,000 $ per 1,000 Weights
 
 

The list-picker rows are the daily editor arms, which choose a handful of postings from a slate rather than scoring each one; their AUC is a coarse pick-or-not score and understates them. Four things the table says that the headline does not. Price does not buy accuracy: the cheapest hosted frontier model lands within a hundredth of the most expensive one from the same lab. Size does not either: the best language model in the table is a local 31B Gemma that needed two hours per thousand postings and 63 GB of disk to finish 0.04 behind a model under one. The configuration matters as much as the model: one 27B model spans 0.72 to 0.86 across its configurations, a wider range than the gap between the best language model and TabPFN. And the only row TabPFN could not separate from, with companies held out, was a single Sonnet 5 run.

The full write-ups, with the method and the per-row intervals, are on my blog: The New Architect Role and The Model That Cannot Write a Sentence.

entry.title: How We Built a Structured AI Readiness Assessment for SAP Customers - Stop Guessing. Start Assessing
entry.content:
Ask ten customers "how ready are you for AI?" and you get ten different answers — all of them based on gut feeling. Some point to a Copilot pilot that ran for three weeks. Others mention their data lake. A few say "we have an AI strategy" but can't tell you who owns it or what it covers. The result: conversations that start from completely different baselines, and recommendations that don't land.

That's the gap a structured AI Readiness Assessment closes.

We designed the assessment around nine dimensions — covering everything from executive strategy and workforce readiness to data foundation, technology infrastructure, and AI governance. Two dimensions are deliberately SAP-specific: the maturity of the SAP landscape itself, and whether there is an actual plan to consume and realize value from SAP's AI capabilities. Generic maturity frameworks miss exactly these.

Each dimension is scored 1–5: from L1 Initial (ad hoc, no structure) to L5 Autonomous Enterprise Ready (AI drives outcomes, full lifecycle in place). A score of 2 isn't a failure — it's a priority signal. What matters is the pattern across all nine axes: where is the organization strong, where is it lagging, and where are the critical gaps?

The assessment runs as a facilitated workshop, not a survey. When a cross-functional group has to agree on a number, the disagreements that surface are themselves a finding. That conversation produces three outputs.

The first is a radar chart — a 9-axis diagram showing current score in blue and target score in green for a 12–18 month horizon. The gap between the two lines is the prioritized action space.

The second is a gap analysis: for each dimension with a delta, concrete actions, ownership (SAP-side vs. customer-side), and effort classification — quick win or strategic initiative.


The third is a benchmark comparison — how does the customer's profile compare to peers at a similar transformation stage. This reframes the conversation from "are we good enough" to "where do we invest next to stay competitive."

 

The Tool Behind It
The assessment runs in a purpose-built Excel workbook with weighted scoring per dimension, plus a companion HTML visualization that renders the radar chart and gap analysis live during the session — no server, no login, no external dependency.

If you're working on something similar or want to adapt this for your own customer engagements, feel free to reach out.

entry.title: The Extended Warehouse Management in SAP S/4HANA FAQ Series: Joule skills in SAP EWM
entry.content:
As many of our EWM customers are excited to learn what AI Joule capabilities are coming in the next releases with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition for EWM, we’ve decided to write this blog to share a little bit of an overview of what newly released features are already available and how customers can get access to them.

What is SAP Joule, and where can I get the latest information on Joule?
We update constantly the official documentation of SAP Joule, and you can always refer to the official documentation here.

What are the different types of skills that Joule is capable of?
In general, there are different interaction patterns that are offered by Joule capabilities:

  • Informational. Joule can understand your questions with human natural languages and provide relevant context regarding the queried SAP business objects.
  • Navigational. Users can ask Joule to help navigate and open the correct FIORI apps and SAP transactions to perform certain business processes.
  • Transactional. Joule can understand the questions and retrieve the necessary business data from the backend SAP system and react on the user instructions to trigger executable steps directly in the backend systems.
  • Analytical. Joule can provide real time analytical views on certain business processes and steps within SAP systems.

In the following paragraphs, we provide a breakdown of each Joule skill.

Joule informational skills in EWM
As part of the centrally delivered Joule skills, it understands automatically also the EWM context and business objects based on trained SAP help documentation. EWM customers can ask any relevant questions, and Joule will be able to search for the data and provide a summary as well as trusted link to the SAP help documentation. The following screenshots provide a simple example on the Joule documentation flow:

 

 Joule navigational skills in SAP EWM
We have enabled EWM navigational Joule skills with some of our frequently-used EWM FIORI apps and SAP GUI for HTML transactions as of 2509 release.

This is particularly useful when we have new users that would like to familiarize themselves with EWM transactions and find the most suitable transactions to perform certain EWM processes. For a list of full Joule EWM navigation capabilities, refer to this SAP Note 3523238, or the official SAP help documentation.

The following screen shots provide an example of EWM Joule navigation flow, where the user would like to create product warehouse tasks:

 

 Note: the default warehouse setting on FIORI also plays a role here, that by navigating to the FIORI app.

Joule transactional skills in EWM – Talk to your warehouse Outbound process
Our first Joule scenario focuses on the Warehouse Outbound process, where the users can get all details of outbound delivery orders (ODOs) on the header and item level. The Joule skills are released according to monthly Joule release calendar in the following phases:

  • 2511 release: read outbound delivery order and item
  • 2512 release: query outbound delivery order and item
  • 2602 release: read warehouse order and tasks, read ODO properties
  • 2605 release: further change actions on the ODO level, including:
    • Create, confirm, cancel pick WO/WT.
    • Invest blocking reasons
    • Set and reverse different status on the ODO, such as “Ready for Shipping” status.
    • Post and reverse post of Goods Issue.

This screen shot gives a peek into how it will look like to interact with Joule for the warehouse outbound process.

 For more information, refer to the SAP help documentation.

Future direction of Joule skills in EWM
We are working closely with our Joule team to enable additional EWM Joule skills to enrich the foundational capabilities of the SAP Joule - EWM integration. As our future development focus will naturally shift to Joule agent enablement, we are working closely with the customers and partners on getting our first agent up and running. We will continue to enable more skills in the future, too.

 Question – where do we get started with Joule?
We would like to recommend our EWM customers to get familiarized with SAP BTP and Joule with the following SAP help documentation link: https://help.sap.com/docs/joule/integrating-joule-with-sap/introduction. It gives detailed information on the initial setup, onboarding, and integrating Joule with SAP solutions (in our case S/4HANA EWM on private cloud).

Question – we are S/4HANA EWM customers, are we entitled to EWM Joule capabilities?
The best way is to check directly with your SAP Account team. As of SAPPHIRE 2026, SAP has announced the AI eligibility with customers running on SAP ECC, or S/4HANA ERP on Premise releases. There might be some further detailed discussions needed, for example to understand from a commercial perspective if you can get a (free or chargeable) subscription to SAP BTP where Joule will be running on, and to understand the technical prerequisites in getting the Joule skills up and running for your business. One example is, we have enhanced our A2X APIs of Warehouse Order/Warehouse Task in the SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS00 (October 2025) release to support some Joule skills, which might not be available in lower releases.

 Question – are there any setup guides on how we can start to enable EWM Joule capabilities?
Follow this SAP Joule Help Documentation: https://help.sap.com/docs/joule/capabilities-guide/activating-business-ai-and-assigning-users

Question – how can I get involved with future Joule skills/agent development roadmap?
You are always welcome to contact us, the EWM product management team directly. We have customers, partners and consultants who work with us along each feature requirement, and we are eager to hear from your team.

In addition, if you are interested in taking part in our combined logistics customer user group (for core logistics, EWM or TM), feel free to leave us a private message with your contacts, and we will forward it to our internal team. We are working actively with our EWM community in getting firsthand feedback on on-going agent development this year, and it’s your chance to influence our EWM future roadmap.

entry.title: Local AI models for ABAP: what you gain and what you pay (measured)
entry.content:
Two reasons keep coming up for running an AI model locally for ABAP work: the client's code never leaves your machine, and there is no bill per token. Both are good reasons. Before recommending it to anyone, I wanted a few numbers from a normal developer PC, not from a 128 GB workstation.

The setup

  • My PC: Ryzen 7 5700X, 24 GB RAM, Radeon RX 580 with 8 GB (an old card; Ollama runs it through Vulkan).
  • Ollama 0.35, local models at temperature 0.
  • Two systems to judge the code: S/4HANA 2023 (ABAP 7.58) and S/4HANA 2020 (ABAP 7.55).

1. Speed: what "zero cost" looks like on this PC

ModelFile sizeTokens per second
ABAP fine-tune, 3B (8-bit)3.3 GB17.3
qwen2.5-coder 7B (4-bit)4.7 GB12.5
qwen2.5-coder 14B (4-bit)9.0 GB5.5

A correct answer to the tasks below is 200 to 900 tokens. With the 7B that is 15 to 70 seconds per answer, with the 14B 40 seconds to almost 3 minutes. The 14B does not fit in 8 GB of video memory: Ollama put a third of it on the CPU (66% GPU, 34% CPU), and that is where the speed goes. I did not try a 32B model: it needs around 20 GB, and this PC has 24 GB of RAM in total.

So there is no bill per token, but the cost does not disappear. It moves to hardware and to waiting time.

2. Quality: does the ABAP compile, and is it right?

I wrote 9 small tasks that look like daily work:

  1. A SALV report on SFLIGHT (the same request as in a local AI tutorial here in the Community)
  2. Last day of the month (date logic)
  3. Sum an internal table by key, modern syntax
  4. ABAP SQL count with a range
  5. Materials with texts, keeping materials without a text (LEFT OUTER JOIN)
  6. ALPHA conversion (leading zeros)
  7. An AMDP method in SQLScript
  8. A CDS view entity with an association and a filtered path
  9. ABAP Cloud: read products through the released API, not table MARA

The judge is the SAP system, not me:

  • Each answer is checked by the ABAP compiler. If there are errors, the compiler message goes back to the model, up to 3 times.
  • The code that compiles is activated, and hidden ABAP Unit tests (the model never sees them) check the result.
  • Task 9 also runs ATC with the variant ABAP_CLOUD_READINESS.
  • Before measuring any model, I tested the judge itself: a correct solution passes every task, and known bugs fail. For example, the language filter in the WHERE instead of the ON turns the outer join into an inner join, and the test catches it.

The local model here is a small ABAP fine-tune (Qwen2 architecture, 3.1B parameters, 8-bit). It fits completely in the graphics card, which is the realistic size for a normal PC. As a reference line I ran the same tasks with a cloud model (Claude Sonnet 5.5).

ModelSystemCompiles at first tryCompiles after compiler feedbackCorrect (hidden tests)
ABAP fine-tune, 3B (local)20232 of 92 of 90 of 9
Claude Sonnet 5.5 (cloud)20238 of 99 of 99 of 9
Claude Sonnet 5.5 (cloud)20207 of 88 of 88 of 8

(Task 9 is only in the 2023 run: ABAP Cloud on-premise starts with S/4HANA 2022.)

How the small model failed is worth a look:

  • Report: it read a table FLIGHTS (the table is SFLIGHT) and called a function module ALV_GRID_DISPLAY that does not exist, with invented parameters. Then it repeated i_grid_border_radius_... until it hit the token limit.
  • Date: it compiled at first try, with a fixed list of month lengths. February always has 28 days, and the month is read from the wrong position of the date. All 5 tests failed.
  • AMDP: it declared the marker interface and then wrote ev_count = SELECT COUNT(*) FROM MARA WHERE MANDT = iv_mandt. That is neither SQLScript nor ABAP.
  • Compiler feedback: it did not help. In the 7 tasks that never compiled, the model answered the compiler message at least twice by sending back exactly the same code.

The cloud model also made one mistake: in the report it forgot the @ before a host variable. The compiler caught it, and the model fixed it in one round.

3. Local is not automatically private

I checked four things on my PC:

  • Where Ollama listens. By default only on 127.0.0.1:11434, and that is what I found. If you set OLLAMA_HOST to 0.0.0.0, anyone on your network can use it.
  • Which websites can call it. The default list is localhost and the editor webviews. One tutorial here sets OLLAMA_ORIGINS="*". With that, any website open in your browser can send prompts to your local model and read the answers.
  • Cloud models. Ollama now also serves cloud models. My server config shows OLLAMA_REMOTES = ollama.com and OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD = false. If you pick a cloud model by mistake, the prompt leaves your machine. OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 switches that off.
  • What leaves during generation. I listed the TCP connections of the Ollama processes while the model was writing: nothing outside the machine. Your editor extension is a separate program, with its own settings and telemetry. Check it too.

And one that has nothing to do with AI: if your SAP password sits in plain text in the editor settings file, that is the leak.

My take

  • If the client's code cannot leave your machine, local is the right direction. The privacy argument is real.
  • A small model that fits a normal graphics card does not write correct ABAP by itself. In this test: 0 of 9.
  • The compiler loop catches mistakes, but it cannot add knowledge. It fixed the cloud model's one slip in one round, and it did not move the small model at all.
  • Whatever model you use, the compiler and a test have to see the code before you trust it.
  • If you go local, use the biggest model your hardware runs at a speed you accept, and check the four points above before you connect it to anything.

Caveats

  • One run per task: local models at temperature 0, the cloud model with its default settings. Another run could give other answers.
  • The small model was measured only on 2023, and its answers were cut at 1,500 tokens (the longest correct answer was under 900).
  • For the 7B and the 14B I measured only speed, on a short answer of about 120 tokens. Their ABAP quality is not in this post.
  • The tasks are small, one object each. No RAP, no enhancements.
  • I could not test Joule, so it is not in the comparison.
  • The cloud model is the reference line, not a recommendation.

Your turn

Are you using a local model for ABAP? Which model, on what hardware, and for what kind of work?

entry.title: SAP Advances Safe and Reliable Enterprise AI with NVIDIA
entry.content:
Co authors: Mayank Shrivatsava, Henning Heitkoetter, Jim Rapp, Lukasz Ostrovski, Johannes Hoffart

The collaboration between SAP and NVIDIA is aimed at solving some of the toughest challenges to ensure enterprises can run AI safely and reliably. By innovating across SAP’s applications and SAP Business AI Platform, our ongoing collaboration is delivering foundational capabilities across governance, data sovereignty, and more.

We are combining NVIDIA accelerated computing, open models, inference software, and secure runtime technologies with SAP’s business data, applications, process context, identity, and governance. The result is a practical foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise, where people set direction and trusted AI helps execute.

Our joint engineering work is already changing what SAP customers can build and deploy. Customers can experience that work firsthand at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, October 20-22, and at SAP TechEd Berlin, October 27-29. During these events, our teams will demonstrate how this partnership is moving AI from experimentation to governed, production-ready business value.

Below, we’ll take a closer look at the six areas where we’ll see these innovations on display. They reflect months of real progress toward SAP and NVIDIA’s vision for enterprise AI, and I hope you’ll join us at NVIDIA GTC Berlin and SAP TechEd in Berlin to see for yourself.

Securing Agent Execution at Enterprise Scale with NVIDIA OpenShell

Enterprise AI agents must be able to act securely inside regulated business processes. SAP has co-development activities and actively contributes to the OpenShell code and embeds OpenShell with SAP Business AI Platform. This deep collaboration is focused on making AI agents in the enterprise safer, more governable, and auditable by design.

Together, we created a hardened runtime environment for enterprise-scale to support industries with strict security and compliance requirements – including regulated industries.  OpenShell’s isolation with the business governance layers from SAP creates the execution boundaries for AI agents requesting access to sensitive data, user access rights, model selection, where the operation runs. Requests that fail any check are blocked before data is touched, and every decision produces an auditable record.

Agents built in Joule Studio are deployed on SAP Business AI Platform where we have embedded OpenShell. For customers who are hesitant to move AI into regulated workflows, this removes the principal architectural blocker.

Advancing Voice Intelligence with NVIDIA Speech Models

A voice agent that sounds good in a demo is not the same as one that really works for a procurement manager on a loud factory floor.

SAP and NVIDIA, together with LiveKit, have built a production voice architecture based on NVIDIA Nemotron speech models. The Nemotron speech models  handle speech-to-text, and NVIDIA Magpie TTS Multilingual handles text-to-speech with streaming inference. Both run inside NVIDIA NIM and are planned for availability SAP voice capabilities in Q4 2026.

The architecture is designed for enterprise reality. Semantic turn detection prevents the agent from cutting off users mid-sentence. Custom vocabulary boosting ensures SAP-specific terminology such as transaction codes, abbreviations, and industry jargon are transcribed and spoken back correctly. Full data residency within the SAP-controlled environment meets the biometric and privacy requirements that voice data demands. Self-hosted open models are not optional here, they are the design constraint. SAP is planning to use this voice architecture in Joule and the Autonomous Suite.

Accelerating SAP HANA Cloud with Vera

SAP and NVIDIA are evaluating the potential of NVIDIA Vera CPUs to accelerate SAP HANA Cloud. Initial testing shows strong performance across analytical and transactional workloads. As Vera becomes available, SAP will continue its testing of NVIDIA Vera to ensure SAP keeps pace with the demands of its enterprise customers.

Closing the Gap Between the Shop Floor and the ERP with NVIDIA Cosmos

Industrial environments require continuous inspection. Today those inspections are manual, infrequent, and inconsistent. Hazards and anomalies go undetected, and findings rarely reach enterprise systems automatically.

SAP’s Physical AI and NVIDIA Cosmos are changing that. Robots, fixed cameras, and drones conduct scheduled inspections while NVIDIA Cosmos Reason analyzes the collected data in real time, identifying findings with location, severity, and confidence scores. The analysis is then directly converted into structured records in SAP S/4HANA, including safety observations with scene descriptions, coordinates, and photographic evidence.

The same architecture extends to asset condition monitoring, production quality, and other inspection domains. At NVIDIA GTC Berlin, visitors can see how a humanoid robot performing a full safety walkthrough can identify a hazard with 95% confidence and create the corresponding SAP record end-to-end.

Tabular AI Accelerated by NVIDIA AI Infrastructure

The majority of SAP’s core business data is structured: tabular data in finance, supply chain, procurement, and HR. Predicting late deliveries, detecting invoice errors, scoring customer churn: these tasks have traditionally leveraged large language models (LLM) or required expensive, time-consuming custom model development that is difficult to scale.

SAP’s tabular foundation models (TFM), including SAP-RPT and TabPFN from Prior Labs, change that equation. Using in-context learning, teams provide example rows and receive predictions instantly with no model training or complex pipelines required. A single model adapts across multiple business scenarios while providing row- and column-level explainability for transparent, auditable results.

Acceleration on NVIDIA AI infrastructure makes these models fast enough for real-time enterprise predictions at scale, accessible through a single managed endpoint on SAP Business AI Platform.

Accessing Best-in-Class Models with SAP AI Core with NVIDIA NIM

Model quality matters, but so does the infrastructure that serves them. NVIDIA NIM microservices provide a standardized, optimized serving layer for connecting to frontier models with SAP AI Core in SAP Business AI Platform on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

Leading models from partners such as Mistral and Cohere are hosted in a SAP or a partner certified datacenter and managed by SAP, meeting regulations such as GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific compliance requirements.

For enterprises, this means access to best-in-class AI under a single SAP contract, with simplified commercial and legal processes and full data residency guarantees. Whether driven by regional policies, regulatory mandates, or internal governance, customers can define and enforce the boundaries of their AI landscape while benefiting from the performance that accelerated NVIDIA infrastructure delivers.

A Conversation Worth Having: Sovereign AI in Europe

At NVIDIA GTC Berlin (Oct 20-22), SAP and NVIDIA are joined by Deutsche Telekom for a dedicated executive panel on AI for the Autonomous Enterprise, with a particular focus on sovereign AI in Europe.

The message is clear: European enterprises do not have to choose between AI ambition and sovereignty.

NVIDIA provides accelerated compute and AI software. SAP provides the enterprise layer: data, workflows, governance, and application integration. Deutsche Telekom contributes trusted European infrastructure.

Together, leaders from these three companies will discuss what production-ready, sovereign AI looks like in practice as a competitive advantage for European organizations ready to execute their AI strategy with trust.

The Autonomous Enterprise Hands-On

This collaborative work is tangible today. At NVIDIA GTC, visitors will also have the chance to create and publish agents in an OpenShell runtime with the Joule Studio activation, watch the Physical AI demo with NVIDIA Cosmos, explore the Tabular AI activation, and experience the OpenShell showcase for secure agent execution.

Just one week after NVIDIA GTC, customers and partners are invited to SAP TechEd Berlin, where SAP Business AI Platform will be on display along with the engineering experts behind it.

The Autonomous Enterprise is being built incrementally, by teams who are innovating to make safe, reliable AI a reality for organizations around the globe. SAP and NVIDIA look forward to partnering with you on the foundation – join us in Berlin!

entry.title: AI Product Management: Evals Are Not the Last Step
entry.content:
Most development frameworks put evaluation at the end. For deterministic software, that was late but recoverable. For agentic AI built with coding agents, it is the wrong sequence, and the cost shows up in production, not in the review.

This is not an argument against evaluation. It is an argument about when evaluation belongs in the process, and what it does when it arrives early instead of late.

The approval problem

"Follow up appropriately on overdue invoices." Give that requirement to a team and ask for a show of hands on approval. Most hands go up.

Now give the team an invoice under dispute. One person expects a reminder. Another expects an escalation. A third expects a hold on all further orders. All three approved the same sentence.

The sentence sounded like an agreement. It was a postponement.

A traditional PRD documents the decision. An eval forces it. Here is the situation. Here is the expected action. Here is how we check it. The ambiguity that survived the requirement review does not survive the first time someone has to write down the expected output.

That "someone" used to be a developer. A developer hitting an ambiguous requirement had options: apply judgment, check the code that handled the adjacent case, send a Slack message to the PM. The ambiguity got resolved human-to-human, often invisibly, often well enough.

Now that someone is a coding agent. A coding agent does not send Slack messages. It resolves ambiguity by making an assumption and proceeding, fluently and at speed, in whichever direction its training makes most plausible. The assumption does not surface as a question. It surfaces as code, and the code ships.

The eval set is the mechanism that makes the assumption explicit before the coding agent encounters it. Not because the agent is worse than the developer. On many dimensions it is faster and more consistent. But it needs clearer guidance than any developer ever did, and it cannot ask for what it does not know it is missing.

This is the first thing an eval set does when it arrives early: it converts speculative agreement into explicit design, before the coding agent begins.

The four moments

An eval set used only before release is a quality gate. An eval set present throughout development is a design instrument. The difference is when it is introduced, not what it contains.

Before development begins. The eval set defines what success means before a single architecture decision is made. It forces the team to be precise about the cases the system must handle, the cases it must not handle, and the cases where the right answer is to stop and ask. That precision changes what gets built.

During development. When trying alternatives is cheap, the eval set replaces the architecture review. Which model, which prompt, which approach handles the hardest cases in the set? The answer is a number, not a preference. Teams that set this up before development begins make better architecture decisions faster than teams that run experiments after the fact.

Before release. The eval set becomes the gate. A failure blocks the release. Not because the team is being cautious, but because the acceptance criteria were defined at the start and the system has not met them.

After launch. The world changes. APIs update. Data drifts. User behavior shifts. The eval set run on a schedule tells you whether the system still behaves as designed, before a customer tells you it doesn't.

What the set should contain

Most evaluation datasets are mostly happy path. The user asks a reasonable question. The system returns the right answer. This is the easiest part of the problem, and passing it is not a finding.

Of the twelve evaluation configurations I ran for a classification project recently, one was the happy path. The other eleven were not: adversarial inputs, edge cases, cases where the rule is technically correct but wrong for the situation, cases where the expected answer is a refusal rather than a response. Those eleven configurations were where the architecture decisions were made. The happy path told me nothing I didn't already know.

The hard cases are where the embedded judgment lives. The PM's job is to put them in the set before development starts, not to discover them in production.

Pass@K and the saturation problem

Because agentic systems are non-deterministic, a single evaluation run is not a result. The correct measure is Pass@K: run the same evaluation K times and report the distribution. Eight to twenty runs for a production evaluation. A system that passes 7 of 10 runs on the hardest cases is a different system from one that passes 10 of 10, and a PRD cannot tell you which you have.

The related problem: a target score is not a destination. When a system consistently passes a high percentage of an eval set, the honest interpretation is that the eval set is no longer hard enough. The benchmark needs to grow as the system improves. A fixed target is a fixed ceiling.

Three deliverables, not one

The PRD can be retired in its traditional form. What replaces it is smaller and more precise.

A short human brief establishes that the problem is worth solving and the investment is justified. It supports the go/no-go decision and nothing more. It does not describe behavior.

A detailed executable brief specifies behavior, authority, exceptions, and what the system does when it encounters something outside its scope. This is where the design work happens, not in prose requirements, but in the explicit definition of each case the system will face. Unlike a PRD written for a developer who can fill the gaps, this brief is written for a system that cannot.

An eval set compares implementations against each other and against the expected behavior defined in the brief. It is the evidence that replaces the assumption. It travels with the system into production and grows harder as the system matures.

The PM owns what good means. Domain experts make it precise. Engineering makes it testable. None of that is new. What is new is that the precision happens before the build, not after, and is expressed in a form the system can be measured against rather than a document it can only approximate.

What this changes

The user story assumed a human would catch what the spec missed. A developer could ask. An agent at runtime cannot. The eval set is the last place the PM's judgment lives before the system acts on its own. Introducing it late means the judgment arrives after the architecture is fixed, the model is chosen, and the hard cases have already been discovered in production.

Less speculative detail to start. More evidence to continue. The eval is how you earn the right to continue.

This post is part of the AI Product Management series on SAP Community. The views expressed here are my own and do not represent the position of my employer.

entry.title: SAP and NVIDIA : Training Compact Instruction-Following Rerankers using OPD (On-Policy Distillation)
entry.content:
Rerankers sit at the center of every retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) stack: a first-stage retriever casts a wide net, and a cross-encoder reranker decides what the LLM actually reads. In enterprise assistants the ranking decision is rarely just about relevance. The right answer may depend on which source is authoritative, which release of a product the user is on, whether a document has been superseded, or how old it is. Instruction-following rerankers address this by accepting a natural-language instruction alongside the query. The strongest instruction-following rerankers, however, are large, and large rerankers are expensive at the latency budgets a production assistant demands.

This post describes how we trained a compact 1B-parameter instruction-following reranker, built on the NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Rerank 1B V2 model, which outperforms its own 4B teacher under distribution shift while running at about a third of the teacher's latency. The key idea, reward-based on-policy distillation over ranking permutations, is the subject of our EMNLP 2026 Findings paper, On-Policy Distillation Meets Off-Policy GRPO: Training Compact Instruction-Following Rerankers. In collaboration with NVIDIA, the resulting model was quantized to NVFP4 with NVIDIA Model Optimizer and is deployed as an NVIDIA NIM microservice on SAP AI Core, where it supports the retrieval pipeline for SAP's Joule for Consultants (J4C) and turns ranking policies such as source prioritization, chronological ordering, negative filtering, and recency filtering into a single instruction rather than a tangle of hand-written rules.

Why Instruction-Following Reranking Matters in the Enterprise

Joule for Consultants retrieves evidence from heterogeneous sources: official SAP Help documentation, SAP Notes and knowledge base articles, customer-specific grounded documents, community content, and the open web. A consultant asking about a configuration step expects the answer to be grounded in the official documentation for their release, not in a three-year-old forum thread that happens to share more keywords. Pure semantic relevance cannot express that preference. An instruction can:

Query: How do I enable the new approval workflow in release 2605?

Instruction: Prefer official SAP Help Portal documentation, then SAP Notes.

Prefer documents for release 2605 or later. Exclude pages marked deprecated or superseded. Down-rank content older than 18 months.

A reranker that follows instructions like this gives the retrieval pipeline a control surface that product teams can change without retraining anything. The question we set out to answer was how to get that capability into a model small enough to run on every request.

The Problem with Offline Distillation

The standard way to shrink a reranker is knowledge distillation: run a strong teacher over a fixed training set, record its scores or pairwise preferences, and train the student to imitate them. This is offline distillation: the student only ever sees supervision on the teacher's own outputs. It never receives feedback on the rankings it would actually produce, so its mistakes on inputs the teacher ranked differently go uncorrected, and any teacher-specific bias is copied verbatim. Both problems get worse under distribution shift, which is exactly where a production reranker spends most of its life.

On-policy distillation has recently become the preferred post-training recipe for reasoning and code models: the student generates its own trajectories and the teacher grades them. We asked whether the same principle holds when the action space is a permutation of candidate documents rather than a sequence of tokens.

A Two-Stage Recipe: Off-Policy Teacher, On-Policy Student

Our pipeline uses the same group relative policy optimization (GRPO) machinery twice, in two different roles (Figure 1). Both stages sample complete rankings with Plackett-Luce sampling and update with group-normalized advantages; they differ only in whose policy generates the rankings and what provides the reward.

Figure 1. The two-stage training pipeline. Stage 1 aligns a 4B ZeRank-2 teacher with LLM-judge rewards (off-policy with respect to the eventual student). Stage 2 distills into a 1B Llama-Nemotron student on-policy: the student samples rankings from its own policy and the frozen teacher scores them.

Stage 1: Strengthen the Teacher with Off-Policy GRPO

We start from ZeRank-2, a 4B open-weight instruction-following reranker. For each of 88,755 training examples (query, instruction, candidate pool), the teacher samples k = 8 rankings from its own Plackett-Luce distribution. An LLM judge scores each ranking, rewards are normalized within the group, and the teacher is updated with a KL penalty to its reference and an entropy bonus. We validated the judge before trusting it: five strong LLM judges agree closely on relevance ordering, and the judge used in training agrees with human relevance labels on 92.6% of a held-out sample (Cohen's kappa = 0.84).

Stage 2: Distill into the Student On-Policy

Here the roles flip. The 1B student samples k = 8 rankings from its own policy. The frozen Stage 1 teacher does not produce rankings. It only scores the candidates, and we rank-normalize those scores into soft relevance labels. Each student-sampled permutation is rewarded with nDCG@6 computed under the teacher's soft relevances, advantages are group-normalized, and the student is updated with a GRPO policy-gradient step plus a KL term to the teacher's first-selection marginal and an entropy bonus. Three epochs of this on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU take under five hours.

The important distinction from offline KD is where the supervision lands: on rankings the student explored, not on a fixed teacher-generated distribution. The student can therefore discover orderings the teacher never emitted and still be rewarded for them when the teacher's scores agree.

Results: The Student Generalizes Better Than Its Teacher

We evaluate on a 9,861-query in-distribution validation set and on MAIR, an out-of-distribution suite spanning web search, scientific, biomedical, financial, and argumentative retrieval. MAIR-11 is the original 11-subset, 869-query benchmark; MAIR-Full covers all 126 tasks and 9,356 queries. Candidate pools are frozen and shared across every method so that only the reranker varies.

MethodValidationMAIR-11 (OOD)MAIR-Full (OOD)
A1 Offline listwise KD0.76080.72120.6564
A10 Offline pairwise RankNet KD0.75140.74160.6521
A2 Teacher-sampled GRPO (off-policy)0.73180.73560.6438
A9 On-policy generalized knowledge distillation (GKD) (distribution matching)0.74760.73860.6657
A3 On-policy GRPO distillation (ours)0.76240.76700.6808

Table 1. nDCG@6 on validation (query-micro average) and the two OOD benchmarks (MAIR-11 query-micro; MAIR-Full task-macro). All variants share the same Stage 1 teacher and the same Llama-Nemotron-1B student backbone.

The headline number is on MAIR-11: on-policy GRPO distillation reaches 0.7670 nDCG@6, +4.58 points over offline listwise KD (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 1.95e-9). The in-distribution gain is small (+0.16); the OOD gain is large. That asymmetry matters: the student is not memorizing the teacher's training-set behavior but learning a more transferable ranking policy. The 1B student also surpasses its own 4B teacher (0.6880 on MAIR-11) and two released 7B RL-trained rerankers, Rank-R1-7B (0.7342) and REARANK-7B (0.7315), evaluated zero-shot on identical candidate pools.

Figure 2. MAIR-11 nDCG@6 with 95% query-bootstrap confidence intervals. A3 is the proposed method; A4 and A5 remove the KL and entropy terms and land within three-seed noise of A3.

What Makes It Work

Two controls isolate the mechanism. A9 (on-policy GKD) keeps student-sampled rankings but replaces the permutation-level reward with teacher-distribution matching; it trails A3 by 2.8 points on MAIR-11, so sampling alone is not enough. A10 (pairwise RankNet KD) changes the offline objective from listwise to pairwise; it helps a little but stays offline and stays behind. A2 samples rankings from the teacher instead of the student and is the weakest variant of all. The combination that wins is specific: student-driven sampling plus a scalar reward on the whole permutation.

Two more results matter for practitioners. Distilling from the unaligned base teacher (0.7412 on MAIR-11) is clearly worse than distilling from the Stage 1 teacher (0.7670), so the teacher strengthening pays for itself. And training on hard labels instead of soft teacher relevances fits the validation set more aggressively but generalizes worse (0.7365 on MAIR-11), so the soft feedback is doing real work.

Distillation Gains Across Student Models

We repeated Stage 2 with the same frozen teacher on three architecturally different students: BGE-Reranker-v2-Gemma, MXBAI-Rerank-Large-v1, and RankZephyr-7B. All three improved on validation (+3.2% to +4.6% nDCG@6) and on MAIR-11, with BGE-Reranker-v2-Gemma gaining 68% on the latter. Our primary student, based on NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Rerank 1B V2, achieved the highest validation nDCG@6 among the four in a compact 1B model. Hyper-parameter sweeps over group size, temperature, KL weight, and entropy coefficient showed little variation in validation performance across the tested settings.

Efficiency: The Distilled 1B Reranker at 9.2 ms

Table 2 reports single-query latency on an NVIDIA H200 under a fixed harness. The distilled 1B student (Distilled-1B in Table 2) averages 9.2 ms per query against 27.0 ms for the 4B teacher (2.9x faster) and sits at the fast end of the open rerankers we compared, with a far tighter tail than the smaller BGE and Jina models. The whole pipeline is inexpensive by today's standards: roughly 195 H200 GPU-hours end to end, dominated by the one-time Stage 1 teacher run (about 4 days on 2 GPUs); the Stage 2 distillation that produces the deployable model takes under 5 hours on one GPU.
